AAAC: Only the highest-rated layer of CLOs, the AAA slice of bundles of business loans, which gets paid first and is last to absorb losses. It aims for income a step above Treasuries with top credit ratings, so the trade-off is complexity rather than obvious credit risk.
ARB: Companies in the middle of being bought out, bought at a small discount to the price the acquirer has agreed to pay. It profits when deals close as planned, a strategy meant to earn steady gains unrelated to the stock market's direction, though a collapsed deal can sting.
ASEA: The 40 largest companies in Southeast Asia across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines, with banks taking nearly two-thirds of the fund. It is a regional bet dominated by Singapore's big banks, so it behaves more like a financial fund than its name suggests.
BGCG: A concentrated portfolio of fast-growing companies outside the US, from Asian chipmakers to Latin American online marketplaces and European luxury and payment firms, with technology about two-fifths. Baillie Gifford picks for long-term growth and holds through ups and downs, so patience is part of the design.
BPRO: Assets meant to gain when paper money loses value: mostly physical gold, with silver, gold mining shares and bitcoin alongside. It is a hedge against currency debasement, the slow erosion of purchasing power, so it is built for fear of inflation and money printing rather than for growth.
BUZZ: US companies generating the most positive chatter online, chosen by scanning social media, news and blogs rather than financial statements. Technology is about half the fund, and the lineup rotates with the conversation, making it a bet on crowd enthusiasm that can turn quickly when sentiment flips.
CCOM: Commodity exposure linked to China, built from futures on raw materials traded in Chinese markets, in a structure designed to avoid K-1 tax forms. It is a niche diversifier for investors who want Chinese commodity prices in a brokerage account, and futures markets can behave differently from the goods themselves.
CHIQ: Chinese consumer companies: online marketplaces, electric car makers, food delivery, travel booking and restaurant chains, nearly all in consumer discretionary. It is a focused bet on China's shoppers, so it moves with Chinese consumer confidence, regulation and the wider China market mood.
FDCF: Companies reinventing how people communicate and consume media: social platforms, streaming services, internet networks and the chipmakers behind them. Communication firms are about half and technology most of the rest, making it a growth bet on the future of media and connectivity rather than the broad market.
GENT: Intermediate-term investment grade bonds, mostly US Treasuries with some corporate debt, chosen with a quality-first approach. It is a core bond holding meant for steady interest income, and because its bonds mature in the middle range, its price moves moderately when interest rates change.
GINX: Dividend-paying companies around the world, banks the biggest slice at about a third, plus an options overlay that sells very short-dated contracts to add extra income. It is built for income first and growth second, and the fast-moving options strategy sets it apart from plain global dividend funds.
GNOM: Companies working with the human genome: gene sequencing, genetic testing, gene-based medicines and the tools labs use to read DNA. It is a focused bet on genomics reshaping medicine, so it rides on scientific breakthroughs and trial results rather than the wider health care market.
GSJY: Japanese companies across every major industry, weighted by four investing factors, value, momentum, quality and low volatility, rather than by size alone. Banks, carmakers, electronics and industrial giants all feature, giving broad Japan exposure with a rules-based twist on the usual index.
HERD: Five Pacer funds under one roof, each hunting companies that generate lots of free cash flow for their size, across US and international markets. The cash cows idea favors profitable, cash-rich firms over fast growers, giving this fund-of-funds a value tilt and an income streak.
HIPS: Up to 40 US-listed securities built to pass their earnings straight to shareholders: energy partnerships, lending firms, property owners and income funds. That pass-through structure produces unusually high income, and it sets the fund apart, though payouts can shrink when energy and credit markets struggle.
HYSD: High yield corporate bonds that come due soon, lending to below-investment-grade companies but only at the short end of the maturity range. Short maturities make its price steadier than a typical junk bond fund when rates move, though the borrowers' default risk remains.
IBBQ: Biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies listed on the Nasdaq, from large drugmakers with approved medicines to smaller firms betting on a single treatment. It is a focused health care bet where trial results and regulators' decisions can swing individual stocks, and the whole fund, sharply.
IBOT: Companies building robots and automation worldwide: factory robot makers, sensor and machine-vision firms, chip designers and industrial software, split between technology and industry. It is a focused bet on machines doing more physical work, tied to factory spending rather than consumer trends.
IFLR: Stocks in developed markets outside the US, banks and industrial firms the biggest slices, paired with options arranged as a floor to limit how far the fund can fall. It aims for international growth with a built-in brake, giving up some upside to keep losses within a managed range.
IMAR: Options on large companies in developed markets outside North America, covering Europe, Japan and Australia, with banks and industrial firms the biggest slices. It is built to absorb a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each March, in exchange for capped gains.
INDS: Real estate companies in warehouses, distribution centers and self-storage, the property types behind online shopping and goods movement. Three big landlords make up nearly half the fund, so it is a concentrated income bet on industrial property rather than the whole real estate market.
ITDE: A retirement fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2045, mixing stock funds from around the world with a smaller slice of bond funds. Its mix automatically grows more cautious as 2045 approaches, shifting from growth toward income and capital preservation over time.
KAMO: A tactical bundle of bond funds, currently parked mostly in very short-term Treasuries, top-rated loan bundles and ultra-short bonds, that can shift toward riskier credit when its managers see opportunity. It aims for income with flexibility, moving between safety and yield as conditions change.
MFSM: Municipal bonds from states, cities, schools and hospitals across the US, actively managed and mostly maturing in the intermediate range. Their interest is exempt from federal income tax, which sets this apart from taxable bond funds and makes it a common choice for higher earners investing outside retirement accounts.
MJ: Cannabis companies from around the world: growers, retailers and makers of medical and recreational marijuana products, plus a large stake in a sister cannabis fund. It is a pure bet on legal cannabis, a young industry where regulation shifts can send the whole fund soaring or sinking.
NFRX: Infrastructure companies picked by active managers: electric and gas utilities are about half, with railroads, pipelines and other transport and energy networks making up the rest. These businesses run essential services with steady demand, so the fund is built as a defensive income-leaning stock holding.
NFTY: India's 50 largest listed companies, held in equal weights so mid-sized names count as much as the giants, across banks, consumer brands, materials and drugmakers. Equal weighting sets it apart from most India funds and makes it a balanced single-country bet on Indian growth.
NUAG: The broad US investment grade bond market, Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt, tilted to squeeze out a bit more yield than a plain core bond fund. It is meant as a portfolio's main bond holding, offering steady income with slightly more credit risk than the plainest version.
OGIG: The world's internet giants, screened for quality and growth: online shopping, search, social media, cloud software and streaming across the US, China and beyond. Technology and communication firms together are over four-fifths of the fund, making it a concentrated bet on the biggest platforms.
OWNS: Government-backed mortgage bonds whose loans were made to minority, lower-income and workforce families and to neighborhoods with persistent poverty. It pays interest like other mortgage bond funds, and it sets itself apart with an affordable housing mission behind every loan it finances.
PSCE: Small US energy companies: oil and gas drillers, equipment and service firms, and pipeline operators outside the industry giants. It is a focused bet on smaller energy names, which swing harder than big oil stocks when fuel prices and drilling activity move.
PSMO: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged under a structured outcome design that cushions a middle range of losses over a period resetting each October. It trades some upside for that moderate protection, aiming for a calmer ride than owning stocks outright.
QCJL: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big non-financial technology and internet companies, with a conservative cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each July. It tempers one of the market's swingiest indexes, trading away some upside for a calmer ride.
RBUF: Options that follow small US companies, mostly in health care, banking, technology and industry, with a buffer built to absorb the first slice of losses each quarter (the 10 in its name). It resets every three months instead of yearly, trading capped gains for frequently renewed protection on small caps.
RIET: One hundred US real estate securities chosen for high dividend yields: warehouse, storage, hotel and casino landlords, plus some preferred shares. It is built purely for property income, so it leans on the highest payers, which can mean more risk when property markets cool.
RSSX: Two strategies stacked in one fund: full exposure to large US stocks, plus an equal second layer split between gold and bitcoin, built with futures. That stacking means every dollar does double duty, which can boost diversification but also magnifies moves in both layers.
RWLC: Large US companies with an active tilt toward businesses seen as next-generation leaders, which leaves technology at over two-fifths of the fund. It is a growth-leaning core holding that reweights away from simply owning the biggest firms, so results can differ noticeably from a plain index fund.
SPD: Large US stocks across every major industry, plus a put options overlay designed to gain value quickly in a sharp crash, which traders call downside convexity. The insurance can pay off in panics, but its cost quietly trims returns during long calm stretches.
SPDV: Large US companies from a major index, screened for dividends that are both high and sustainable, then held in equal weights. It is an income-tilted value fund, so it favors steady payers like energy, retail and tech hardware firms over the fastest growers.
TDSC: A shifting mix of stock sector funds, bonds, real estate and gold, managed to keep losses in a bad stretch near its 10 percent drawdown target. It is a moderate, defense-minded allocation fund that steps toward safety when markets wobble, accepting smaller gains in strong rallies.
TISC: Hundreds of small companies outside the US, spread thinly across Europe, Japan and other developed markets, with industrial firms the biggest slice at about a quarter. It offers the small-company growth effect abroad, where less analyst coverage can mean more mispricing and more volatility.
TMFM: Mid-sized US companies picked for quality and growth by the Motley Fool team, spread across technology, health care, industry and finance in a focused portfolio. It is an active growth fund whose results depend on a few dozen stock picks, so it can stray well away from index returns.
TOAK: An absolute return strategy built entirely from defined-risk options, meaning long calls, puts and debit spreads where the most any position can lose is the premium paid for it. It keeps overall duration between zero and one year, which is why it sits among ultrashort bond funds despite holding no ordinary bonds.
TRSY: US Treasury debt maturing within a year, the closest thing to cash that still pays a little interest. Investors use it to park money safely for short periods, and its price barely budges when interest rates move, unlike longer-term bond funds.
UDN: A futures bet that the US dollar will fall against six major currencies, the euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona and Swiss franc. It rises when the dollar weakens, so traders use it as a hedge or a short-term wager, and futures-based funds fit brief holding periods best.
WEEI: Nothing but energy companies, and mostly the giants: the two biggest US oil majors alone are well over a third of the fund, with refiners, drillers and pipeline firms behind them. It is built for income from oil and gas, so it rises and falls with energy prices and dividends.
XV: Short-term government investments paired with an options spread strategy, built to pay monthly distributions at a target annual rate, the 15 in its name. The payout is the whole point, so it suits income seekers, though the distribution rate is a goal rather than a promise.
ZJAN: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each January. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZNOV: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each November. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
ZOCT: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to protect against losses over a one-year outcome period that resets each October. In exchange for that defined protection it gives up gains beyond a preset cap, so it suits investors who fear a downturn more than missing a rally.
